narrative:
The model estimates a 42% chance that you will leave your job. That is not a certainty, but it is a substantial retention risk, and in this promotion decision it was enough to deny the promotion. The prediction did not use your gender, age or health information.

The strongest signal was your total years of experience. You have 11+ years, well above the 14.7% share among employees predicted to stay, and this pushed the model toward leaving—suggesting that highly experienced employees may be more mobile or harder to retain. The second, and strongest countervailing, signal was the number of training programmes you attended in the last three years. You attended 7+, more than most employees predicted to stay, and this pushed toward staying, indicating the organisation’s development investment may increase attachment. Third, your time in the current organisation is in the one-to-five-year band; in your profile this pushed toward leaving, implying that despite broad experience, your roots in this particular role or organisation are not yet strong enough to offset the risk.

Other context matters: your emotional commitment is low (only 10.1% of stayers are in that group), and you do not feel you received the promotion you deserved. Before the decision is final, the organisation should discuss transparent promotion criteria, a concrete career path and retention plan with you, and make better use of the training and recognition you have already received. You should seek clear feedback on what would change the outcome and decide whether the growth you need is available here.
